html:
The Second Vatican Council, or Vatican II, was the meeting of the world's Catholic bishops in Rome from 1962 to 1965 that modernised the Catholic Church. It met in four autumn sessions in St Peter's Basilica, with more than two thousand bishops taking part.

Pope John XXIII called it, saying the Church needed to update itself for the modern world. He died in 1963, and Pope Paul VI led the last three sessions and approved its sixteen documents.

What changed:

  • The Mass could be said in local languages instead of only Latin, and lay people took a bigger part in worship.
  • The Church took a warmer stance toward other Christians, after centuries of hostility since the Reformation.
  • It declared respect for other religions, and rejected blaming the Jewish people as a whole for the death of Jesus.
  • It backed religious freedom as a right of every person.

It was the first general council since 1870, and the largest in the Church's history. Its meaning is still argued over. Some Catholics feel it did not go far enough, while traditionalists feel it went too far and still prefer the old Latin Mass. Later popes, among them John Paul II, who attended as a young bishop, and Francis, have presented their work as carrying the council forward.
